explanation: No single trigger. It fires on a mix of tokens: subword pieces in the middle of a word ('ac' in ultracold, 'á' in Bhriocáin, 'us' in Vinnicius), the colon after 'Category' in wiki footers, and some ordinary words in running text ('tweets', 'conditional', 'United', 'the'). Hard to predict for a new token.

Strongest on words for the outcome of a sports match ('losing', 'eliminated', 'beaten', 'loss', 'came out on top', '1st set', 'visit'). It also fires on unrelated tokens such as 'port'/'ports' (network or USB), 'Rabies' and 'senescence'.

Fires on subword fragments inside rare, foreign or technical words: chemical names (-O, icos, chloro), Latin species names, Hungarian/Turkish text, and pieces of names (Bho-jpuri, Mont-ic-ello, lady-in-w-aiting). There are scattered exceptions on common English words ('ass', 'positive', 'is').

A mixture: French verb and word pieces, subword fragments of proper names (Guggenheim, Monash, Ceballos), whitespace and indentation tokens in legal captions and code, and some English verbs ('take', 'come'). No clear shared feature.

Words for physically mixing or agitating substances, strongest on 'stirring', 'shake', 'mixed', 'mixing'. Weaker on nearby process context in recipes, chemistry and materials text (emulsions, suspensions, 'mechanically', 'mixture', melt-processing).

A mixture. It fires on 'file' in Apache license headers ('this file'), on names and pronouns at the start of a sentence or clause (Derek, Brian, he, she), on variable tokens in code and math problems, and on assignment targets like 'result'.

Mostly nouns or verbs inside technical error messages and software help questions ('SQL syntax', 'ERROR: function', 'cannot load', 'unused_imports', 'Subsystem'), plus generic nouns for things that vary or are constrained ('unit', 'variables', 'factors', 'depending'). The pattern is loose.

Mostly code and technical identifier tokens: LLVM '@', '{' in Haskell records, SQL keywords like FAST/PARTITIONED, file-format and module names (WMV, .transform, md, keyup). It also fires on legal 'WRIT' and some prose nouns ('schedule', 'minorities', 'analog').

Mostly the second or later subword piece of a proper name or compound (Mc-Kin-lay, Sw-iss, Aub-urn, Sub-strate, KTLO-FM, up-regulated). It also fires on the '--' after a TV-station dateline and a few other tokens. Several jobs.

A mixture. It fires on the adverb 'just' ('just because', 'just yet', 'just in case'), on digits inside U.S. statute section numbers (28 U.S.C. § 2254, 9541), and on a variety of nouns in news text ('percent', 'crimes', 'people', 'goals').

No coherent pattern. It fires on assorted nouns ('motion', 'round', 'source', 'age', 'conclusion'), symbols in code and statistics ('=', '**', 'dydt', 'SQLSTATE'), digits inside numbers, and pieces of words.
No coherent pattern. It fires on assorted nouns ('thing', 'percent', 'reason(s)', 'Manager', 'Wars', 'Opportunity'), pieces of names (Cauchy, Comer), LaTeX/R tokens like '\dots', and acronym pieces.

A mixture. It fires on technical and medical adjective suffixes ('pathological', 'hepatic', 'metallurgical', pyrolysis), on compass or side words in descriptions of places ('south', 'north', 'left'), on integral subscripts '_{' in LaTeX, and on some prepositions in scientific prose.

Loosely, negation or quantifier words that start a noun phrase ('no one', 'line no', 'could not', 'little or no', 'these', 'one element', 'almost none'). It is mixed with chemistry and technical noun pieces ('bond', 'resin', 'PAGE', 'spectrometry') and commas.

A mixture. It fires on a number or unit token after a quantity ('6 cyl', 'cd', 'm', '5D'), on prepositions in descriptive text ('from', 'of', 'de'), on code punctuation, and on name pieces. No clear shared feature.

Two jobs. Mainly it fires on '=' in code and math assignments or equations (MATLAB, LLVM, math word problems) and on 'by' in 'Code generated by'. Second, it fires on the comma or last subword piece of personal names in attorney and author lists ('Ziccardi,', 'Sanchez,', 'Potencier').
The punctuation token that opens an inline citation marker right after a claim in scientific or wiki text: ' ([', '.[', ',[', '[@', '.^'. It fires weakly on other brackets and punctuation.

Apostrophes and quote marks that are encoded or escaped oddly ('""', '\'', "''", 'ʹ', '?s', mojibake) inside possessives and contractions. Weaker on other odd separators: spaced ' .' and ' ,', the middle dot as a decimal point, and en dashes.

Line-break tokens (often with '.', ',' or ');') that end a line inside a source-code comment header, especially license or auto-generated boilerplate, where the next line continues the comment with // or #. Weak on line breaks in ordinary prose.

Concrete nouns and adjectives for physical appearance, texture or material in descriptive writing ('eyebrows', 'brow', 'crunchy', 'glued', 'rubber', 'garlic', 'spherical', 'velcro', 'crochet', 'fingers'). Weak or none on abstract words and code.

A mixture of formulaic slots: 'the term' in patents ('As used herein, the term'), 'The population' in stubs about places, boilerplate license words ('either express', 'this permission notice', 'Before you'), 'generated by', and connectives like 'Not only' and 'In addition to'.
